newsitem.title: USA: UK wins G7 support over Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: UK wins G7 support over Hong Kong.

text.p: The Group of Seven rich nations and Russia expect China to uphold its commitment to preserve civil liberties in Hong Kong when it regains control of the British colony on July 1, officials said on Saturday.

They said a communique being drafted by the G7 and Russia at a summit here also "looked forward" to China holding democratic elections for a new legislature in Hong Kong as soon as possible after the handover.
British officials, keen for international backing for their campaign to hold China to account over Hong Kong, said they were pleased with the strong message of the communique.

But they said they had won no assurances that other governments would follow Britain and the United States in boycotting the ceremonial inauguration of the Beijing-appointed provisional legislature that will replace the current elected Legislative Council in the early hours of July 1.
The communique said Russia and the G7 -- the United States, Britain, Japan, France, Italy, Germany and Canada -- welcome and "place weight" on commitments given by China.

"These include ensuring Hong Kong's continued stability and prosperity and preserving its way of life, its high degree of autonomy -- including an independent monetary and economic system -- its fundamental freedoms and the rule of law.
"These will provide the essential underpinnings for Hong Kong's future economic success," the draft communique says.
British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said Britain, the colonial power for more than 150 years, had prime moral responsibility to ensure China kept its word on Hong Kong.
But he said it was not helpful to threaten sanctions if Beijing failed to honour its commitments under the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration covering the handover.
"We don't want to get the best possible range of sanctions when it goes wrong. We want to stop it from going wrong," Cook told reporters.
But he said Britain would closely monitor events after June 30 and would be looking for international support if civil liberties in Hong Kong were curtailed.

"That is why it is important that we do now pin down the world community with commitments that are contained in the communique to support the present level of freedom and prosperity of Hong Kong," Cook said.
In particular, he said G7 foreign ministers had agreed that China should be judged by its promise to hold free and fair elections to a new Legislative Council within 12 months.
"It is very important that China does keep to that timetable and that commitment and that, I think, will be the focus of a lot of international concern and monitoring," Cook said.

He said he and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright would boycott the inauguration of the provisional legislature because by attending they would have bestowed legitimacy on an undemocratic body.
Cook said he did not expect they would be alone in their boycott but avoided a direct answer when asked whether France and Germany would be absent.
"It is for others to decide what they do on that occasion. What is important is that they should join us in the pressure on China to hold new elections," Cook said.
